h1: Fair Value Gaps (FVG): Formation, CE and Examples
quickAnswer: A fair value gap (FVG) is a three-candle price imbalance. In a bullish FVG, the high of candle 1 sits below the low of candle 3, so the middle candle's strong move left a price range that the outer candles never covered. Traders mark that range as a zone, watch its midpoint (called consequent encroachment, or CE), and look for price to return to it as potential support or resistance. In a bearish FVG, the low of candle 1 sits above the high of candle 3.
takeaways: An FVG is a zone, not a single line. It is defined by two prices: the wick of candle 1 and the wick of candle 3.
It records one-sided, fast trading. It is a footprint of displacement, not a guarantee of anything.
CE is the 50% midpoint of the gap. Many traders treat it as a verdict line for whether the gap is respected.
A gap can be tapped, partly filled, fully filled or inverted (turned into the opposite zone). Each state means something different.
Not every FVG fills, and not every FVG is worth trading. Size, location, timeframe and trend context decide quality.
FVGs work best as one piece of a confluence stack, together with structure, liquidity and higher-timeframe bias.

sections.title: 1. What Is a Fair Value Gap?

blocks.text: When a market moves very fast in one direction, price can race through a range so quickly that the candles around the move never trade in part of it. On the chart, that leftover stretch looks like empty space beside a long candle. Traders call it a fair value gap, imbalance or inefficiency.

The idea behind it: that range saw trading mostly from one side (urgent buyers or urgent sellers) and little from the other. Many traders expect price to come back later to "rebalance" that area, and they use the returning visit as a place to plan entries, stops and targets.

Beginner picture: Imagine a sale where shoppers rush a shelf so quickly that several price tags are skipped without anyone checking them. Later, some shoppers drift back to look at what they missed. An FVG is that skipped shelf on a chart.

Name warning: "Fair value" also has other meanings in finance, such as an estimate of what an asset is worth, or the theoretical level of a futures contract against its index. The chart-pattern FVG in this guide is different. It describes a skipped price range, not a valuation.
An FVG needs three consecutive candles. The middle candle is the engine (the displacement). The outer two define the edges.

Bullish FVG                      Bearish FVG
          [C3] low  ---- top of gap          [C1] low  ---- top of gap
   [C2]    |  (gap zone)                      |  (gap zone)
          [C1] high ---- bottom of gap       [C3] high ---- bottom of gap

rows: High of C1 is below low of C3
Low of C1 is above high of C3
Low of C3 minus high of C1
Low of C1 minus high of C3
Possible support (price dips in, then rises)
Possible resistance (price rallies in, then falls)

blocks.text: Rules of thumb for drawing it

items: Use wicks, not bodies, for the edges. Gaps between bodies where wicks still overlap are a different thing (volume imbalance, see Section 10).
Look for a large middle candle. A tiny middle candle with a small gap is usually noise.
Draw the box from candle 1's wick edge to candle 3's wick edge, then extend it to the right until it is resolved.
Mark the midpoint (CE) with a dashed line.

blocks.text: Three common triggers produce the fast, one-sided move that leaves a gap:

rows: A burst of market orders eats through the available quotes faster than new quotes appear
A surprise changes expectations instantly; both sides reprice
Few resting orders, so a modest order skips several price levels
Off-hours, holidays, small caps, low-volume crypto pairs

blocks.text: Also common: stop-order cascades, where triggered stops become market orders and accelerate the move, and liquidity sweeps, where price grabs resting orders above a high or below a low and then reverses with force.
The "return to rebalance" theory, and its honest limits

The popular explanation is that the unmatched range holds unfinished business, and that liquidity providers prefer to trade at every price, so price tends to revisit it. It is an appealing story and it fits many charts. Keep two cautions in mind:

items: It is a working theory, not a measured law. Several educational sources themselves say the pattern does not prove institutional involvement and cannot predict reversals.

Because FVGs are everywhere on charts, you will always find examples that worked. The real question is how often they work compared with a rule you set before the trade. Section 18 explains how to test that.

sections.title: 4. Bullish and Bearish FVGs (BISI and SIBI)

blocks.text: In Inner Circle Trader (ICT) terminology the two types have longer names that describe who was active:

rows: A bullish FVG. Buyers dominated; sellers barely traded in the gap
A bearish FVG. Sellers dominated; buyers barely traded in the gap

blocks.text: A simple memory trick: the first word names the side that was pushing price. BISI means buyers pushed. SIBI means sellers pushed.
How traders read each type

items: Bullish FVG in an uptrend: a pullback into the gap is a candidate buy area.
Bearish FVG in a downtrend: a rally into the gap is a candidate sell area.
Opposite-direction FVGs can also act as targets, since price often travels toward the next unfilled gap.

blocks.text: Consequent encroachment (CE) is the exact midpoint (50%) of the FVG. Some call it the mean threshold.
Formula: CE = (gap top + gap bottom) / 2
Why traders care about CE

rows: Price that dips into the gap but stays above CE (bullish) is read as respecting the gap. A close beyond CE is read as weakening it
Some traders place limit entries at CE for a tighter stop and better reward-to-risk, accepting that price may not reach it
"The gap filled to CE" is a standard way to describe depth of retracement
Many models call a gap "mitigated enough" once CE is touched

blocks.text: Three CE outcomes to know

items: Holds: price touches or slightly pierces CE and reverses. Gap respected.
Wicks through, closes back: price spikes beyond CE but candles close back inside the gap's favourable half. Often read as a stop hunt followed by respect.
Closes through: a candle closes beyond CE (or the far edge, depending on the rule). The gap is weakened or, if closed fully through, may invert (Section 9).

blocks.text: Traders disagree on whether to use the CE or the far edge for invalidation. Pick one rule, write it down, and test it. Do not switch rules mid-trade.

sections.title: 6. The Life Cycle of an FVG

blocks.text: A gap changes state as price interacts with it. Knowing the state tells you what to expect.

rows: Gap formed; price has not returned
First reaction point; many entries trigger here
Price entered but did not cross the far edge
Zone may still have remaining reactions
Price traded through the entire gap
Price reacted and moved away in the original direction
Price closed through the gap against its direction
Price never returns and keeps going

blocks.text: The prices below are made up to show the arithmetic. They are not real market data.
Example A: Bullish FVG and a CE entry

items: C1 high (100.00) is below C3 low (102.00), so a bullish FVG exists.
Later price pulls back to 101.00 and prints a bullish rejection candle.
A trader using CE as entry might place a stop just below the gap bottom, at 99.60, and a target at the prior swing high of 106.50.
Risk = 101.00 − 99.60 = 1.40. Reward = 106.50 − 101.00 = 5.50. Reward-to-risk is about 3.9 to 1.

blocks.text: Example B: Bearish FVG, filled edge to edge

items: C1 low is 250.00, C3 high is 247.50, so a bearish FVG from 247.50 to 250.00 exists. CE = 248.75.

Price rallies, passes CE, and closes above 250.00. The gap is fully filled and the original selling pressure is questioned. A trader who needed the gap to hold is stopped out. This is why rules for invalidation matter.

blocks.text: Example C: Not an FVG

items: C1 high is 80.00 and C3 low is 79.60. The wicks overlap, so no FVG exists, even if the middle candle is large. Do not draw a zone.

blocks.text: Example D: Breakaway gap

items: A bullish FVG forms at 40.00 to 41.50 on a strong earnings reaction. Price keeps rising for days without returning. The gap never fills in the trader's window. Waiting for a pullback would have meant no trade, which is a normal outcome and a reason to never chase.

blocks.text: Example E: Crypto illustration (concept only)

A coin jumps through a price band in one candle with almost no trading inside the band. That band is the FVG. If price later returns to the midpoint and bounces, traders describe it as a CE respect. If it slices through on high volume, they treat it as a failed gap.

FVG sits inside continuous trading and uses three candles
Often used as synonyms for FVG; "imbalance" can also mean any lopsided area
A larger stretch of fast, thin trading, often covering several candles
FVG is a small, precise three-candle version; a void can contain several FVGs
Gap between candle bodies while wicks still overlap
Price technically traded there, just one-sidedly; weaker signal than an FVG
Last opposite candle before a strong move

Similar flip idea to an inverted FVG

blocks.text: Gap vs FVG in one line: a regular gap needs a break in time (market closed, then reopened); an FVG needs only speed.

An inverse fair value gap, also called an inversion FVG or IFVG, appears when price returns to an FVG and closes through it instead of respecting it. The failed zone is then treated as a zone of the opposite type.

rows: A candle closes below the gap
Later rallies into it may reverse down
A candle closes above the gap
Later dips into it may reverse up

blocks.text: Why the flip idea makes sense: traders who bought inside the original zone are now trapped. When price comes back up to their entry area, some exit at break-even, which adds selling pressure. This is the same logic behind "broken support becomes resistance."
Rules that different teachers use (pick and test one)

rows: Candle body closes beyond the far edge
Not required; the flip can come after several candles
Some require it within a few candles
Close on a lower timeframe is accepted by some
Retest of the new zone's CE

blocks.text: Typical IFVG sequence

items: Price forms a bullish FVG and starts to rise.
A liquidity sweep or news event drives price back down.
A strong candle closes below the bullish FVG.
Price retraces up into the now-inverted zone and stalls near CE.
A rejection candle gives the entry; stop above the zone; target is a prior low or the next opposing FVG.

blocks.text: Important: inversion gaps are rarer and more selective than normal FVGs, and they work best with other evidence (structure break, liquidity sweep). Trading every inversion without filters tends to look like random noise.

blocks.text: Most charts contain dozens of FVGs. Trading all of them is the fastest way to give back profits. Score each gap against this checklist.

rows: Gap is meaningful against recent average range (e.g. a multiple of ATR)
Tiny gap that disappears inside the spread
Gap agrees with the higher-timeframe bias
Bullish gap in a discount (lower half of the swing); bearish gap in a premium (upper half)
Bullish gap in premium, bearish in discount
Created while breaking a swing high/low (market structure shift)
Follows a sweep of equal highs/lows or a prior high/low
Forms in a liquid session or key time window
Formed on scheduled data; treat with care around releases

blocks.text: A simple scoring habit: give each gap one point per filter, trade only gaps with a minimum score, and test whether higher scores really produce better results.

rows: Decide whether you only look for buys or sells; mark large FVGs as targets
Find the FVG you want price to reach
Wait for a lower-timeframe confirmation (structure shift, inverse FVG, rejection candle) inside the area

blocks.text: Useful ideas:

items: Higher-timeframe FVGs are stronger and last longer. A daily gap can stay relevant for weeks.
A lower-timeframe FVG inside a higher-timeframe FVG is a classic nested setup.
Opposing HTF gap = target. Price is often drawn toward an unfilled gap in the direction of bias.
Do not mix rules between timeframes without testing; a rule that works on the 1-hour may not on the 1-minute.

blocks.text: A generic step-by-step plan (works for strategies 1 to 3)

items: Bias: decide direction from a higher timeframe.
Level: note a liquidity level (prior high/low, equal highs/lows) price may sweep.
Displacement: wait for a strong move that breaks structure and leaves an FVG.
Mark: draw the zone, its CE, and the swing low/high behind it.
Wait: let price come back. No retest means no trade.
Trigger: require a lower-timeframe confirmation inside the zone.
Execute: enter with predefined stop and target.
Manage: move the stop only by rules you wrote down in advance.
Log: screenshot and record the outcome for later review.

blocks.text: Placement options

rows: Beyond the far edge of the gap
Beyond the swing point that created the gap
Often too tight; zones behave like areas, not lines
Prior day high/low or session extremes

blocks.text: Position-size example (illustrative)

items: Account: 10,000. Risk per trade: 1% = 100.
Entry 101.00, stop 99.60, so risk per unit = 1.40.
Size = 100 / 1.40 = about 71 units.
If the target is 106.50, the potential gain is about 5.50 × 71 = 390.5, so reward-to-risk is roughly 3.9 to 1.
Remember to subtract spreads, commissions and slippage, and note that a high reward-to-risk ratio does not matter if the win rate is too low. Check both numbers together.

blocks.text: Risk rules worth writing down

items: Maximum risk per trade and per day.
No trade inside high-impact news windows unless that is a tested part of your plan.
A maximum number of attempts per gap.
What happens if the gap is filled before your entry (cancel the order).

blocks.text: Treat the FVG as one layer. Each extra layer should add independent information, not repeat the same idea.

rows: Break of structure or change of character
Buy low, sell high within range
Prior day high/low, session open, VWAP, round numbers
Footprint or volume profile (a gap inside a low-volume area tends to be crossed quickly)

blocks.text: Caution: adding more layers does not make a trade safer if the layers all say the same thing. It also reduces how often you trade. Test the stack.

rows: Very liquid majors; FVGs common on news and session opens (London, New York)
Spread widening around news; broker price feed differences
Clean volume data; strong session structure
Open/close auctions create their own gaps
Both FVGs and regular overnight gaps
Earnings gaps are regular gaps, not FVGs; thin small caps produce noisy gaps
24/7 so no session gaps; frequent fast impulses

Strong reaction to inventory and supply reports

blocks.text: Because different brokers and exchanges feed different prices, the same FVG can look slightly different. Draw gaps from the feed you actually trade.

sections.title: 17. Detecting FVGs: Manual, Indicator and Code

blocks.text: Manual steps

items: Scan for large-bodied candles.
Check the candle before and after for non-overlapping wicks.
Draw the box and CE line, extend right.
Mark the state (fresh, tapped, filled).

blocks.text: Indicator features to look for

items: Minimum gap size or ATR filter.
Automatic CE line.
Mitigation rule options (CE touch, close through, full fill).
Multi-timeframe display.
Inversion (IFVG) handling.
Limit on number of visible gaps.
Alerts and backtest-friendly outputs.

blocks.text: Plain-language detection logic (pseudo-code)

for each candle i (starting at the third candle):
    c1 = candle[i-2]; c3 = candle[i]
    if c1.high < c3.low:   bullish FVG, bottom = c1.high, top = c3.low
    if c1.low  > c3.high:  bearish FVG, top = c1.low, bottom = c3.high
    require (top - bottom) >= minimum size (e.g. a fraction of ATR)
    CE = (top + bottom) / 2
    track state: fresh, tapped, CE tested, filled, inverted
Look-ahead warning: the gap only exists once candle 3 has closed. Code or charts that mark it earlier use information from the future and give fake backtest results.

rows: Write the exact rules (what counts as a gap, entry, stop, target, time window) before testing

Track win rate, average reward-to-risk, expectancy, maximum drawdown and trade count
Compare against a simple baseline (e.g. random entries with the same stop and target)
Forward-test on a demo account before risking money

blocks.text: What the evidence honestly looks like: the three-candle shape is easy to measure, so it is easy to test. Many educational authors report that gaps often get revisited and some never are. That is a description, not proof of profit. The pattern appears constantly on every chart, so only strict rules and proper testing can tell you whether it adds an edge for your market and timeframe.

sections.title: 25. Final Thoughts

blocks.text: A fair value gap is a simple shape with a lot of vocabulary built around it. The core idea fits on one line: fast, one-sided trading leaves a zone, and price sometimes comes back to it. Everything else in this guide (CE, inversion, balanced ranges, filters, confluence) exists to decide which gaps matter and what you do when price returns. Learn the shape, write strict rules, test them, and keep risk small.

faqs.question: What is a fair value gap?
faqs.answer: A fair value gap is a three-candle imbalance in which the wicks of the first and third candles do not overlap, leaving a price range that the middle candle crossed rapidly. Traders mark it as a zone and watch for price to revisit it.

faqs.question: What does FVG stand for?
faqs.answer: Fair value gap.

faqs.question: How do you find a bullish FVG?
faqs.answer: Look for three candles where the high of the first is lower than the low of the third. The space between those two prices is the gap.

faqs.question: How do you find a bearish FVG?
faqs.answer: Look for three candles where the low of the first is higher than the high of the third.

faqs.question: What is consequent encroachment (CE)?
faqs.answer: The midpoint of an FVG. Traders use it as a decision line and sometimes as a limit-entry level.

faqs.question: What is an inverse fair value gap (IFVG)?
faqs.answer: An FVG that price has closed through, after which traders treat the zone as the opposite type: a failed bullish FVG may act as resistance, and a failed bearish FVG may act as support.

faqs.question: What do BISI and SIBI mean?
faqs.answer: BISI is a bullish FVG (buy-side imbalance, sell-side inefficiency). SIBI is a bearish FVG (sell-side imbalance, buy-side inefficiency).

faqs.question: Do all fair value gaps get filled?
faqs.answer: No. Many get revisited, some only partly, and some never. Gaps close to current price are revisited more often than distant ones, but there is no guarantee.

faqs.question: How long does it take for an FVG to fill?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed time. Lower-timeframe gaps may fill within minutes or hours; higher-timeframe gaps can last for weeks or longer.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an FVG and a regular gap?
faqs.answer: A regular gap is empty space between one candle's close and the next candle's open, usually after a market closes. An FVG forms during continuous trading and is defined by three candles.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an FVG and a liquidity void?
faqs.answer: A liquidity void is a larger stretch of rapid, thin trading, often spanning several candles. An FVG is the precise three-candle version, and one void may contain several FVGs.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an FVG and a volume imbalance?
faqs.answer: A volume imbalance is a gap between candle bodies where the wicks still overlap, so price did trade there. An FVG requires the wicks themselves not to overlap.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an FVG and an order block?
faqs.answer: An order block is a candle (the last opposite candle before a strong move). An FVG is the gap the move leaves. They are often used together.

faqs.question: Which timeframe is best for FVGs?
faqs.answer: No single timeframe is best. Higher timeframes give stronger, longer-lasting gaps; lower timeframes give more signals but more noise and cost. Many traders use a higher timeframe for bias and a lower one for entries.

faqs.question: Where do I place my stop loss on an FVG trade?
faqs.answer: Common choices are beyond the far edge of the gap or beyond the swing point that created it. Treat the FVG as a zone, not a line, and size the trade so the stop distance fits your risk limit.

faqs.question: Is the FVG strategy profitable?
faqs.answer: No pattern guarantees profit. Results depend on rules, market, costs and risk control. Test your exact ruleset with out-of-sample data before trading real money.

faqs.question: Do FVGs work in crypto, forex and stocks?
faqs.answer: They can appear in any market with candlestick charts. Liquidity, spreads, sessions and data quality differ, so test per market.

faqs.question: Do FVGs work in a sideways market?
faqs.answer: Usually less well. They are most useful after strong displacement in a trending move.

faqs.question: Can I use an FVG indicator instead of drawing by hand?
faqs.answer: Yes. Indicators save time, but check how they define a gap, how they mark mitigation and whether they repaint or use future candles.

faqs.question: Are FVGs related to Smart Money Concepts (SMC) and ICT?
faqs.answer: Yes. They are widely taught in those frameworks, which also teach CE, BISI/SIBI and inversion. The frameworks' claims about institutional behaviour are not proven by the pattern itself.

faqs.question: Can beginners trade FVGs?
faqs.answer: Beginners can learn to identify them and practise on a demo account. Start with simple rules, small risk and a trading journal.
